prompt.context: Our client is Freedom Bikes, the US-based producer of mountain bikes – luxury sport bikes that represent the American spirit of freedom. The bikes are fully designed and manufactured in the US and are sold mainly to US customers, who value independence, freedom, and high quality of a US-based manufacturer. The client has brought us to help decrease costs, which have increased in recent years and eroded the client's margins.
prompt.question: The client asks us to look only at costs — no revenue or profit considerations are necessary. There is no fixed savings target; the more we save, the better. How would you approach identifying and reducing the client's costs?

clarifying_info.a: Overseas sales make up only 10% of operations and can be ignored for this case.

clarifying_info.q: Is the client open to outsourcing manufacturing or sourcing parts from outside the US?
clarifying_info.a: No. Customers value the US-made image, so the client will not consider outsourcing or sourcing even from Canada.
There are two major competitors — one from Japan and one from Italy. Freedom Bikes is the only US-based producer.

clarifying_info.q: What cost reduction target are we working toward?
clarifying_info.a: There is no fixed target; maximize savings wherever possible.

exhibits.title: Freedom Bikes Cost Categories (2009–2013)
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar chart showing total annual costs in USD millions from 2009 to 2013, broken down by cost category.
exhibits.data: Categories: Overhead, Sales and promotion, Distribution, Inventory, Manufacturing, Raw materials. Total bar grows from roughly 200M to nearly 300M over the period, with Manufacturing visibly increasing while other bars remain relatively stable.

exhibits.title: 2013 Manufacturing Costs by Factory (USD Mil)
exhibits.shows: Table of 2013 manufacturing costs split between Michigan and Tennessee factories, plus a process flow diagram showing the production sequence.
exhibits.data: Cost category | Michigan | Tennessee: Workers salaries 16 | 6; Overhead and administration 1 | 1; Painting 1 | 0; Chrome plating 0 | 50; Raw materials processing 2 | 23; Re-work* 0 | 20; Total 20 | 100. Footnote: *75% of re-work expenses caused by chrome-plating operations. Process flow: Tennessee (Processing of Raw materials → Production of assembly kits) → Michigan (Assembly to order of bikes).

exhibits.title: Benchmarking of Chrome-Plating Contractors
exhibits.shows: Comparison table of five potential chrome-plating suppliers across location, cost index, and quality index.
exhibits.data: Supplier | Location | Cost Index | Quality Index: Freedom Bikes (in-house) Tennessee USA 100 100; Magna Ontario CAN 95 130; SACI Shanghai CHN 45 105; Tenneco Tennessee USA 110 140; MetMex Tijuana MEX 100 120; Delphi Michigan USA 135 145. Footnote: *Operations with Quality Index above 120 fully eliminate the need for re-work.

framework: Map all cost categories and identify which are rising vs. stable (use Exhibit 1 to prioritize)
Dismiss cost lines that cannot be reduced: overhead (already slim), raw materials (hedged in bulk), sales & promotion (small fixed), distribution (small and stable)
Identify Manufacturing as the only rising cost requiring attention
Drill into manufacturing by factory and cost sub-category (Exhibit 2) — apply 80/20 to pinpoint the largest line item
Focus on Chrome-plating (Tennessee, $50M) as the dominant cost driver; note that poor chrome quality also drives 75% of Re-work ($20M × 75% = $15M)
Evaluate outsourcing options for chrome-plating — client constraint: US-based suppliers only
Recommend Tenneco (US, Tennessee, Quality Index 140 > 120 threshold eliminating rework) and quantify net cost impact

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, which cost categories should we focus on and why?
questions.guidance: Strong answer applies 80/20: Manufacturing is the largest and only growing category. All other categories (overhead, sales & promotion, distribution, raw materials, inventory) are either small, stable, or cannot be further reduced per client constraints. Therefore, Manufacturing is the clear priority.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 shows 2013 manufacturing costs by factory. What do you observe, and where would you focus?
questions.guidance: Tennessee total ($100M) is 5× Michigan ($20M). Within Tennessee, Chrome-plating ($50M) is the single largest line item — 50% of Tennessee costs and 42% of total manufacturing. Re-work ($20M) is the second-largest and is 75% caused by chrome-plating. Together these two items total $65M and are directly linked. The student should immediately flag Chrome-plating as the 80/20 target.

questions.prompt: Given that improving chrome-plating quality in-house is not feasible, should the client outsource this operation? Use Exhibit 3 to evaluate the options.
questions.guidance: Client constraint eliminates non-US suppliers (Magna = Canada, SACI = China, MetMex = Mexico). Remaining US options: Tenneco (Tennessee, Cost Index 110, Quality Index 140) and Delphi (Michigan, Cost Index 135, Quality Index 145). Tenneco is preferred: lower cost than Delphi, quality above the 120 threshold (eliminating rework), and located in Tennessee near the client's factory (minimizing transport costs).

questions.prompt: Calculate the net cost impact of outsourcing chrome-plating to Tenneco.
questions.guidance: The student should calculate Tenneco's cost relative to current in-house cost, then subtract savings from eliminated rework. Net saving = rework savings minus cost premium.

math.setup: Current in-house chrome-plating cost = $50M (index 100). Tenneco cost index = 110, so Tenneco cost = $50M × 110% = $55M (cost increase of $5M). Re-work currently = $20M, of which 75% is caused by chrome-plating = $15M. Tenneco quality index > 120, so rework is fully eliminated, saving $15M.
math.answer: Net saving of $10M per year by outsourcing chrome-plating to Tenneco.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks should the client consider when outsourcing chrome-plating to Tenneco, and how can they be mitigated?

categories.name: Labor / HR risks
ideas: Elimination of chrome-plating jobs at Tennessee factory may cause labor unrest
Union pressure (note: Tennessee is a right-to-work state, mitigating union risk somewhat)
Risk mitigated by migration of affected workers to Tenneco or redeployment

categories.name: Production / supply chain disruption
ideas: Parts must be transported to Tenneco and back; logistics planning required
Supplier concentration risk if Tenneco has capacity or quality issues
Transition period before full outsourcing is complete may temporarily affect output

categories.name: Quality and brand risk
ideas: Although Tenneco's quality index is high, any defect affects premium US-brand image
Need SLA and quality audits built into the outsourcing contract

categories.name: Strategic / long-term
ideas: Loss of in-house chrome-plating know-how is irreversible

recommendation: Outsource chrome-plating operations to Tenneco (Tennessee, USA), which is US-based (satisfying the client's manufacturing image requirement), located near the Tennessee factory (minimizing transport costs), and has a Quality Index of 140 — above the 120 threshold that fully eliminates re-work costs
Net annual savings: $10M ($15M rework elimination minus $5M outsourcing cost premium)
This preserves the client's US-made brand positioning and the skilled Michigan workforce while addressing the primary driver of rising manufacturing costs
risks: Labor disruption from elimination of chrome-plating roles at Tennessee — mitigate by facilitating worker transfers to Tenneco
Production disruption during transition — mitigate with phased cutover and buffer inventory
Logistics complexity of moving parts to/from Tenneco — mitigate with dedicated transport agreements
Loss of in-house chrome-plating capability — acceptable given client cannot improve the operation internally
next_steps: Negotiate outsourcing contract with Tenneco including quality SLA and pricing
Develop transition plan with phased migration to minimize production disruption
Establish logistics protocol for part movement between Tennessee factory and Tenneco
Communicate workforce transition plan to Tennessee employees
Monitor quality metrics post-transition to ensure rework is fully eliminated
